Strict inequalities by those integers give b < 1−k/(2j) and b > (k−2ℓ)/(2(ℓ+1)). The first forces j > k/2, hence ℓ < k/2 and the integer inequality k−ℓ ≥ ℓ+1. Using j ≤ k−ℓ and the positive numerator k−2ℓ makes the upper bound at most the strict lower bound. This includes k=1, b=0 and b=1/2.

For a > 0 and x ∈ (0,1], the inclusive target count is exactly k+1 with k=min(m,floor((1−x)/a)). If k=0, L_0 alone suffices. For k≥1 the two lower floor arguments are nonnegative since θ≥b, and at most k since θ≤1−b and θ<1≤1+b. Therefore floor-plus-one counts do not reach beyond m. Replacing θ by 1/2 only lowers them and gives precisely the two floor arguments already bounded. For a=0 all entries are 1 and the surplus is m+1.

Each positive entry is at most 1 and each target is nonnegative by am≤1. The finite layer integral with weight p x^(p−1) yields the clipped positive powers for every p>0. A zero entry contributes neither at x>0 nor to the integral, including when am=1.

With m=0, L_0=ρ_0=1 and the remaining power vanishes exactly when ab≥θ, even though a has no upper bound. With m≥1 and a>0, one has a≤1. If b<θ, the interval (1−a,B_0] has positive length, lies in (0,1], and has count surplus at least one. Otherwise b=θ=1/2 and L agrees entry by entry with ρ. The B_0 power is positive unless a=1, which forces m=1. At that endpoint B_h≤0 throughout, so equality holds for all p>0.
